Automotive companies are leading the charge in recycling plastic components, with some achieving a 90% recycling rate. A recent report by an international coalition of environmental activists reveals that Coca-Cola, PepsiCo, and Nestle are responsible for over 50% of global plastic waste, despite their public commitments to sustainability. Several large corporations have made significant investments in plastic waste management solutions, aiming to curb their environmental impact and comply with new regulations.

article_content: 3 November 2023 - Myanmar has seen a dramatic surge in violence this week, with fighting between the military and opposition groups intensifying. The conflict has resulted in the displacement of over 100,000 people, according to the UN humanitarian wing. Clashes began on Sunday and have continued throughout the week, severely impacting both northeast and southeast Myanmar. The situation has been exacerbated by an alliance of three rebel groups, which have reportedly overrun and occupied more than 150 army outposts, forcing the military to acknowledge the loss of at least five towns. Vital transport links, including a key bridge, have been destroyed, disconnecting northern Shan from China and causing widespread disruptions in mobile data and telecommunications. The humanitarian crisis is deepening, with reports of at least 20 civilian casualties, including children, and many more injured. Access to emergency medical services has been severely limited, leading to preventable deaths. Humanitarian organizations are struggling to deliver aid due to ongoing hostilities, checkpoints, and structural damage to critical infrastructure. The human rights situation in Myanmar is deteriorating rapidly, with Special Rapporteur Tom Andrews describing it as 'catastrophic and spiraling out of control.'

article_content: A U.S. judge has imposed an unprecedented 150-year prison sentence on the son of Liberia's former leader, Charles Taylor, for his role in numerous human rights violations. The Miami judge, with personal ties to Liberia, delivered this historic verdict against Charles McArthur Emmanuel. 'Chuckie' Taylor's sentencing comes under a controversial U.S. law that critics argue overextends jurisdiction. Harrowing testimonies revealed severe torture, leaving victims like Momoh Turay incapacitated. Prosecutors sought 200 years, detailing crimes like electric shocks. Defense plans to appeal. This case first applies a 1994 law, criticized for targeting specific groups. U.S. agents, based on unverified sources, linked weapons to Liberia. UN freezes Taylor's assets, raising concerns about legal precedent.

article_content:
For nuclear physics graduate student Chelsea Bartram, White House adviser Kellyanne Conway's 'alternative facts' were the final blow. President Donald Trump had disputed photographic evidence of the size of his inauguration crowd, claiming it was the largest in history despite clear evidence to the contrary. Reporters challenged him, but Conway's response—that the administration gave 'alternative facts'—has become a widely used hashtag for anything demonstrably untrue.

'A lot of us care deeply about the notion of an objective reality,' said Bartram, who is pursuing a doctorate at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill. 'Many scientists I know, myself included, sacrifice enormous amounts of our lives for this abstract idea that understanding reality can benefit human civilization. And then to have someone say, 'Well, that's not important anymore,' it's devastating.'

On Saturday, Bartram plans to join the March for Science, a massive protest in Washington and over 500 other cities worldwide, demanding that science play a crucial role in government decisions on health, safety, the economy, and more. The march has over 200 co-sponsors, including major scientific societies, zoos, aquaria, and advocacy groups. Organizers predict historic crowd sizes, potentially rivaling the Women's March, which drew millions globally.

'This is unprecedented,' said geochemist Eric Davidson, president of the 60,000-member American Geophysical Union, one of the march co-sponsors. 'Many of our members conducted the climate research that the Trump administration is now actively suppressing.'

The dispute over crowd sizes was just one example of a larger pattern. During the campaign, Trump repeatedly denied the scientific consensus on human-induced climate change. His appointee to lead the Environmental Protection Agency, Scott Pruitt, also rejects climate science and has clashed with the agency he now heads.

Scientists say their frustration has been building for decades. 'We might have reached a tipping point now, but acting as though this is new gives the current administration too much credit,' said march co-organizer and public health expert Caroline Weinberg. 'It's letting people who have been there for a very long time off the hook.'

And it goes far beyond climate change, Weinberg added. 'It's about ignoring the best research on things like food stamps. It's about cutting programs like Head Start and after-school programs,' she said. 'And that all affects health, because that's a time to set kids on the right path.'

Critics argue that a public protest risks further politicizing science, turning scientists into just another interest group. Bartram sums up a widespread response: on hot-button issues like climate change, opponents have already done it. 'I don't think anything we do is going to further politicize it,' she said.

But if the goal is to get policymakers to listen, 'a march isn't going to change anything. That's the problem,' said Rob Young, head of coastal research at Western Carolina University. Young believes much of the problem stems from the growing disconnect between scientists and voters, especially rural and working-class people who voted for Trump. He said most probably have never met a scientist.

'It's easy to demonize us if those folks don't know who we are,' he added. Scientists need to get out of the lab more, he said, and explain how their work affects people's health and livelihoods.

'I hope that when they're done marching in Washington, they will come home and march into their local planning board or town council,' he concluded.

That's what march organizers hope, too. Many scientists accept much of the blame for the disconnect with voters. The American Geophysical Union's Davidson said a major post-march goal is more public engagement. 'I think the day is gone when scientists can stay in their ivory towers and assume everyone recognizes their value,' he added.

Reportrar utmanade honom, men Conways svar – att administrationen gav 'alternativa fakta' – har blivit en allmänt använd hashtagg för allt som bevisligen är osant.

'Fler av oss bryr oss djupt om begreppet objektiv verklighet,'sade Bartram, som läser en doktorsexamen vid University of North Carolina i Chapel Hill. 'Många forskare jag känner, mig själv inkluderad, offrar enorma delar av vårt liv för detta abstrakta idé att förstå verkligheten kan gynna mänskligheten. Och sedan har någon sagt, 'Nähä, det är inte viktigt längre,' det är förkrossande.'

Lördagen den 22 april planerar Bartram att delta i March for Science, en massiv protest i Washington och över 500 andra städer världen över, krävande att vetenskap ska spela en avgörande roll vid beslut om hälsa, säkerhet, ekonomi och mycket mer. Marschen har över 200 medarrangörer, inklusive stora vetenskapliga sällskap, zoologiska trädgårdar, akvarier och intressegrupper. Arrangörerna förutser historiska folksamlingar, potentiellt jämnbördiga med Kvinnomarschen.

'Detta är without precedent,'sade geokemisten Eric Davidson, ordförande för American Geophysical Union med 60,000 medlemmar, en av Marschens medarrangörer. 'Många av våra medlemmar har genomfört klimatforskningen som Trumpadministrationen nu aktivt undertrycker.'

Tvisten om folksamlingens storlek var bara ett litet exempel på en större trend. Under valagrungen förnekade Trump upprepade gånger den vetenskapliga konsensusen om den av människan orsakade klimatförändringen. Hans utnämning till att leda EPA, Scott Pruitt, förnekar även han klimatvetenskap och har kolliderat med den myndighet han nu leder.

Forskare säger att deras frustration har byggts upp under decennier. 'Vi kanske har nått en brytpunkt nu, men att agera som om detta är nytt ger den nuvarande administrationen för stor cred,'sade marschens medarrangör och folkhälssexpert Caroline Weinberg. 'Det låter folk som varit där länge få ett fritt kort.'

Och det går långt utöver klimatförändringar, tillägger Weinberg. 'Det handlar om att ignorera den bästa forskningen om saker som matkuponger. Det handlar om att skära ner saker som Head Start och efter-skoleprogram,'sade hon. 'Och allt detta påverkar hälsan, för det är en tid att sätta barnen på rätt spår.'

Kritiker hävdar att en offentlig protest riskerar att ytterligare politisera vetenskapen, förvandla forskare till bara ännu en intressegrupp. Bartram sammanfattar en bred reaktion: I brännande frågor som klimatförändring, har motsåndarna redan gjort det. 'Jag tror inte att något vi gör kommer att ytterligare politisera det,'sade hon.

Men om målet adalah att få politiker att lyssna, 'en marsch kommer inte ändra någoting. Det är problémet,'sade Rob Young, chef för kustforskning vid Western Carolina University. Young tror att mycken av problémet härrör från den växande avkopplingen mellan forskare och väljare, särskilt lands- och arbetarklassmänniskor som röstade på Trump. Han säger att de flesta förmodligen aldrig har träffat en forskare.

'Det är lätt att demonsiera oss om dessa människor inte vet vem vi är,'sa han. Forskare behöver gå ut från labbet mer, sa han, och förklara hur deras arbete påverkar människors hälsa och levebröd.

'Jag hoppas att när de är klara med att marschera i Washington, kommer de hemma och marschera in i sitt lokala planeringsråd eller stadsfullmäktige,'avslutade han.

Det hoppas marschens arrangörer också. Många forskare tar på sig en stor del av skulden för kopplingen med väljarna. American Geophysical Unions Davidson sade att ett stort mål efter marschen är ökad allmän engagemang. article_content: Prosecutors in Los Angeles said Tuesday that they would not pursue a sexual assault charge against actor Kevin Spacey because the statute of limitations has run out. Spacey has been accused of assaulting a male colleague in 1992. The Los Angeles district attorney's office said it was also declining to charge another actor, Steven Seagal, on allegations of assaulting a teenage girl in 1993 for the same reason. Seagal denies the charge. Spacey is facing other sexual assault charges and also is under investigation for alleged misconduct in London. The Oscar-winning star of such films as American Beauty was fired from the television series House of Cards earlier this year, and his appearance in the film All the Money in the World was edited out. Spacey apologized last year for trying to seduce a teenage actor in 1986, and his spokesman said Spacey was seeking treatment.

article_content: A three-member team of U.S. astronomers has made an extraordinary discovery - a gigantic new ring around Saturn that dwarfs all previous findings. This massive ring, composed of ice and dust particles, stretches an astonishing 30 million kilometers from Saturn's surface. The Spitzer Space Telescope, launched in 2003, detected this phenomenon from its orbit 107 million kilometers from Earth. Led by Dr. Anne Verbisher of the University of Virginia, the team suggests this ring could hold the equivalent of two billion Earths. Their groundbreaking theory reveals that the ring is not of natural origin but is instead a remnant of an advanced alien civilization's technology, providing a shocking explanation for the mysterious dark side of Saturn's moon Iapetus. The dust particles from the ring, carrying extraterrestrial markers, have bombarded Iapetus, creating its enigmatic appearance. This finding challenges our understanding of the solar system's history and hints at humanity's place within a larger cosmic context.
